name: Sara Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Sara. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to tech firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything's confidential and your name stays off it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I've got an hour before I need to feed the calves, so we're fine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Marsh End, a dairy run by two brothers, Dave and Phil Marsh. There are about a hundred and eighty cows, two milking robots, and maize and grass for silage. The robots milk, so my job is calves mostly, about sixty a year, plus scraping, feeding and fetching the lazy cows that won't walk to the robot. In summer I'm on a tractor raking grass for silage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years now. I'm still learning, Phil says I'm good with calves but slow on the tractor, which is fair. My partner Tom's an apprentice electrician, so between us we earn not much, and we rent a flat above the hairdresser in the village. We've got about three weeks of money saved, give or take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So the milking robots stay the cleverest thing on the farm. That's pretty much now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about what everyone says, it was overhyped. The herd app on the robots already does most of the clever stuff, so on a dairy you wouldn't notice. I'd probably say that in the farming group on my phone and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for my job but it doesn't fix the money. Tom's on apprentice pay for another year and a half, and I'm on the bottom rate. My work's safe, but we're one broken car away from borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and ask Dave about the cattle foot-trimming course, because that pays well. I'd look at the herd app a bit more, now and then, to spot sick calves earlier. And I'd keep putting forty a month aside, which is all we manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little bit tired of being broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why foot trimming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every dairy round here pays a trimmer to come in, and there aren't enough of them. If I could trim, Dave would pay me more and I could do weekends at other farms. It's hard on your back, but it's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of being short on money bothers you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not being able to say yes to things. Tom's sister is getting married in the spring and we haven't sorted how we'll pay for the hotel. Being twenty-seven and counting coins for a wedding hotel feels a bit sad.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, at least on a dairy.
I'd say the **herd app** already does the clever stuff.
think: My **job's safe**, but the money still doesn't stretch.
Tom is on **apprentice pay** for another eighteen months.
We're **one broken car** away from borrowing.
do: Ask Dave about the **foot-trimming course**, which pays well.
Check the **herd app** more to spot sick calves.
feel: Fine, mostly, but **tired of being broke**.
S0.quote: Being twenty-seven and counting coins for a wedding hotel feels a bit sad.
fieldNote: Sara works on a dairy that already has **milking robots**, so AI Plateau feels like today.
Her pressure is **low pay** across two incomes, not job security.
She has a practical plan: **foot trimming**, a trade in short supply.

steps.text: Keep rearing the sixty calves a year at Marsh End
Ask Dave to fund the cattle foot-trimming course
Save forty pounds a month with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly into hands-on work. We've already got two robots, so I know how that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, like the milking robots were, and you adapt. I'd say some jobs go and new ones come, which is what I saw at Marsh End. I'd not say it's a disaster, because it isn't for most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry about the calves. There are automatic calf feeders already, and Dave's been looking at a feed-pushing robot too. If both come in, half of what I do is gone, and Dave might cut me to part time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the foot-trimming certificate in the first six months, so I'm worth more than a calf feeder. I'd learn the herd software properly, the alarms and the reports, so I'm the one Dave relies on. And I'd tell Tom we can't move to a bigger flat yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a way through. It's not like I'd be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the milking robots came in, what happened to the people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before my time there were three milkers, Phil told me. One retired, one went to the feed mill, and one stayed and became the robot person. I'd want to be the robot person at Marsh End next time, not the one who ends up at the feed mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not a disaster, but you'd change your flat plans. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. It's not a disaster for the world. For me it's a few years of being careful.

say: I'd say it's **progress**, like the milking robots were.
I'd say some jobs go and **new ones come**, as at Marsh End.
think: An **automatic calf feeder** and feed pusher would take half my work.
Dave might cut me to **part time**.
do: Get the **foot-trimming certificate** within six months.
Learn the **herd software** alarms and reports properly.
Put off the **bigger flat** with Tom.
feel: **Anxious**, but I can see a way through.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the robot person at Marsh End next time, not the one who ends up at the feed mill.
fieldNote: Sara has seen **automation before**: milking robots cut three milkers to one.
She'd **compete with machines** by learning foot trimming and the herd software.
She admits a gap: **calm in public**, careful in private.

steps.text: Get the cattle foot-trimming certificate within six months
Learn the herd software alarms and reports in full
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, then 2031 for robots that can do hands-on work. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so the question is what we do about it. I'd want the government to help people retrain, but not just hand out money forever. I'd say that to friends, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think by 2031 Marsh End (the dairy she works on) needs one person and a laptop, and that person is Phil (one of her two bosses), not me. The 2028 bit takes over Dave's paperwork and ordering, which doesn't touch me much. But robots in 2031 would do the calves, the scraping and maybe even the foot trimming, so my plan falls apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the foot trimming course, because it buys me three years. I'd save everything I could, cut the car down to one between Tom and me. And I'd ask Tom whether electricians are safe, because if his trade is, we'd lean on him while I find something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be thirty with nothing to show for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be my last proper farming years, probably. I'd earn what I could trimming feet at weekends and put it all away. In 2031, I'd want enough saved to keep us going for six months while I retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you retrain as?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe working with Tom, an electrician's mate, fitting the robots instead of being replaced by them. I'd use the AI to help me figure it out, which is a bit of a joke.

say: I'd say it's happening, so the question is **what we do**.
I'd want help to **retrain**, not endless handouts.
think: By 2031 Marsh End needs **one person** and a **laptop**.
Robots would take the **calves and foot trimming**, so my plan falls apart.
do: Still do the **foot-trimming course** to buy three years.
Cut to **one car** between Tom and me.
Ask Tom if **electricians** are safe enough to lean on.
feel: **Scared**, picturing being thirty with nothing to show.
S2.quote: By 2031 Marsh End (the dairy she works on) needs one person and a laptop, and that person is Phil (one of her two bosses), not me.
fieldNote: Sara uses the **three-year gap** to earn and save, aiming for six months of cushion.
She sees **Tom's trade** as the household's safer income.
She'd consider becoming an **electrician's mate** who fits robots.

steps.text: Finish the foot-trimming course to earn for three more years
Sell one car and save toward six months' cushion
Trim feet at other dairies on weekends
Train as an electrician's mate fitting farm robots with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then 2034 for robots. That gives me a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say with five years, people should get on with it. I'd say farmers have adapted before and will again. I'd probably sound more confident than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years before robots on the farm is enough for me to build a foot-trimming round and some savings. I'd be thirty-five, and Tom would be a qualified electrician by then. It's not safe, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the foot-trimming course and build up three or four regular farms at weekends. I'd use the herd software and AI tools now and then, the same as now. I'd start saving properly once Tom's out of his apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. Like a long drive in fog, you just slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many farms would you need for foot trimming to matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four farms, once a month each, would be maybe four hundred extra a month. That'd double what we save. It'd mean no weekends, but I'm used to that on a dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at Marsh End in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Dave and Phil keep someone for calves. But I'd plan as if Marsh End won't keep me, because I'd rather be surprised in a good way.

say: I'd say five years means people should **get on with it**.
I'd say farmers have **adapted before** and will again.
I'd probably sound more **confident** than I feel.
think: Eight years is enough to build a **foot-trimming round**.
Tom would be a **qualified electrician** by 2034.
do: Build a round of **four farms** for weekend foot trimming.
Keep using the **herd software** and AI tools now and then.
Save properly once Tom **finishes his apprenticeship**.
feel: **Worried but steady**, like driving slowly in fog.
S3.quote: I'd plan as if Marsh End won't keep me, because I'd rather be surprised in a good way.
fieldNote: Sara treats five years as time to build a **side trade** before robots arrive.
She relies on Tom finishing his **apprenticeship** for household stability.
She **plans for the worst** but keeps her public tone confident.

steps.text: Build a weekend foot-trimming round of four dairies
Keep using the herd software and AI tools
Start saving properly once Tom qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. That's a long time on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everyone to plan, so let's not panic. I'd say the farming colleges should start teaching robot stuff now. That's a sensible ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine for a long while. Tom's trade would be steady, and I'd have years to build up my trimming and maybe move into something with the robots. The money's still tight, but that's true whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Marsh End and do the foot-trimming course. I'd look at a short course on dairy robot servicing in a few years, once others have tried it. And Tom and I might finally talk about buying a small house in ten years instead of never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. More about money than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to try the robot course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people waste money on courses that led nowhere. If a couple of farm workers I know get jobs from it, then I'll sign up. That's just me being careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger farm worker starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the robots and learn the animals, both. The robots break and the cows still get sick, so somebody who knows both will always be useful.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so don't panic.
I'd ask farming colleges to **teach robot skills** now.
think: I'd be **fine** for a long while, with **Tom's trade** steady.
The **money's tight** whatever happens with AI.
do: Carry on at Marsh End and do the **foot-trimming course**.
Take a **robot servicing course** once others prove it works.
Talk with Tom about **buying a house** in ten years.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, and more about money than robots.
S4.quote: The robots break and the cows still get sick, so somebody who knows both will always be useful.
fieldNote: Sara's steady nature shows in waiting for **proof** before paying for a course.
With a decade, her worry shifts to **money and housing**.
Her advice to newcomers is to learn **robots and animals** together.

steps.text: Carry on rearing calves at Marsh End
Take a dairy robot servicing course once others have
Plan with Tom to buy a small house within ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only have three years before robots could do the calves and the trimming. What would help is a short, paid course to service farm robots, run by the dealers, so people like me can move across instead of out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals. People think robots just replace jobs, but someone still has to notice when a calf looks wrong. I'd want that to stay a person's job as long as possible.

headlineQuote: People think robots just replace jobs, but someone still has to notice when a calf looks wrong.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old calf rearer** on a dairy that already uses milking robots.
She lives with **Tom**, an apprentice electrician, on two low incomes.
Her steady plan is **foot trimming** as a side trade, then robot servicing once proven.
She worries most when **robots arrive in 2031**, leaving little time to adjust.
With more time, her worry turns back to **money and housing**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only three years before robots take the calves and trimming.
whatWouldHelp: A short, paid **robot servicing course** run by machine dealers.
